title: Air India Wants More Wide-Body Jets, Eyes Profitability Very Soon
excerpt: New CEO Tewolde Gebremariam says the existing order book is not enough for the airline's network ambitions, as costs, losses and airspace closures squeeze the Tata Group turnaround.
body:
• Air India wants to increase its wide-body aircraft orders beyond the 80 already on order, CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said on Tuesday, without giving numbers or a timeline.
  • Gebremariam, the former Ethiopian Airlines chief who took charge in October, said the Tata Group carrier would return to profitability "very soon" but set no date.
  • Costs are the immediate problem: the airline's cost per available seat kilometre exceeds its revenue per available seat kilometre, and a cross-functional team has been set up to cut costs.
  • For travellers: more Europe and U.S. services will shift from Delhi to Mumbai because of Pakistani airspace restrictions, and Bengaluru is being considered as a third hub.

Air India wants to increase its order for wide-body aircraft as it seeks to boost international passenger traffic, Chief Executive Tewolde Gebremariam said on Tuesday, adding that the Tata Group-owned carrier would return to profitability "very soon." "We want more wide-body aircraft," Gebremariam said, according to Reuters. The comments come months after the former head of Ethiopian Airlines took charge of an airline grappling with higher operating costs, geopolitical disruptions and losses.

More long-haul jets, no numbers yet

Gebremariam told the Aviation India and South Asia 2026 summit in New Delhi that Air India is talking to Airbus and Boeing about increasing its wide-body orders, despite an already substantial order book. "Our network, our strategy demands more," he said, without specifying aircraft types, numbers or a timeline, The Hindu BusinessLine reported. The airline's orders announced in 2023 and 2024 included 80 wide-body aircraft — 50 Airbus A350s, 20 Boeing 787s and 10 Boeing 777Xs — and it added 30 Boeing 737 MAX narrow-body jets in January 2026. An industry source told Reuters the airline is weighing the cost of running its older wide-body jets: "The cost of operating old wide-bodies is high, and they're not very efficient." Since returning to Tata Group ownership in 2022, Air India has run a multi-billion-dollar transformation covering fleet renewal, cabin upgrades and network expansion.

Profitability "very soon" — with costs first

Asked when the airline would return to profitability, Gebremariam said: "Very soon, I would say," without specifying a timeline. "I'm more impatient than the shareholders to see profitability," he added. The urgency reflects the numbers behind the turnaround: BusinessLine reported that Air India Group's consolidated net loss widened to more than ₹6,000 crore in the first quarter of FY27, against over ₹3,000 crore a year earlier, amid foreign exchange fluctuations, elevated fuel costs and airspace closures. Gebremariam said the airline's cost per available seat kilometre exceeds its revenue per available seat kilometre, and correcting that imbalance is an immediate priority, though he said it was too early to set a numerical cost-reduction target. A cross-functional team is examining costs across Air India and Air India Express, including shared corporate functions.

"Efficiency, efficiency, efficiency. That's the name of the game."

Hubs shift west, Bengaluru in play

The network is being rebalanced around the closure of Pakistani airspace, which weighs more heavily on operations from Delhi than from Mumbai. More Europe and America services will move to Mumbai, while Delhi keeps those markets and leads growth towards the east and south-east, where routes are unaffected. Gebremariam said the airline is considering Bengaluru as a third hub alongside Delhi and Mumbai, and argued India could build multiple international gateways able to compete with Gulf carriers. Connecting traffic through India currently accounts for around 10% and could eventually grow to up to 50% as the network expands, he said. Capturing more diaspora traffic, he added, would require global-standard products, stronger network connectivity and a customer-focused business. Both Air India and Air India Express will grow, he said, with the larger share of future growth expected from the full-service, wide-body long-haul business, while Air India Express serves the lower-priced segment.
